newsitem.title: USA: Donors pledge broad financial assistance for Ukraine.
newsitem.headline: Donors pledge broad financial assistance for Ukraine.

text.p: A group of international donors gave Ukraine's economic reform efforts a strong push on Tuesday with the promise of well over $5 billion in assistance over the next three years if the country stayed the course.

The donor nations and international financial institutions pledged some $2.5 billion in basic financing for next year, but a U.S. Treasury official said that with World Bank project loans and other trade credits, the total could be 3.5 billion in that period alone.
Treasury Assistant Secretary David Lipton said the basic financing alone over three years could be about $5.0 billion if Ukraine presses ahead on the reform path.
Such basic funding is used to help a country balance its books with its foreign trading partners and creditors, meeting interest payments on its debt and paying for its imports.
Lipton said that of the $2.5 billion, $1 billion would come from the International Monetary Fund with an additional $1 billion being provided by the IMF over the next two years.

"This is an effort that is quite extraordinary for the international financial community (that it) hopes will support an important ratcheting up of economic and budgetary adjustment and reform in Ukraine," Lipton said.
Monetary sources have suggested that approval of Ukraine's assistance may partly hinge on the reception that its ambitious reform and budget plans receive from its left-dominated parliament.
"I would like to stress that (the IMF and World Bank) elements of the program are conditional," Lipton said, "In other words the funds being pledged will be available only if the reforms go forward."
Lipton declined to say which countries contributed but said he believed the U.S. pledge for so-called balance of payments assistance alone would amount to about $95 million next year.
The pledges by the donor nations and international financial institutions follows Monday's decision by International Monetary Fund to release some $200 million in credits for the country.
The IMF money was being made available under a $867 million stand-by loan agreement struck earlier this year.
The nine-month pact is due to expire in February and Ukraine has been seeking a $2.5-$3 billion, three-year Extended Fund Facility (EFF) credit to replace it.

The government's draft budget, agreed with the IMF, forecasts a 1997 deficit of 5.5 percent of gross domestic product -- four percent by Western calculations -- and forsees inflation at 25 percent, down from 40 percent this year.
The decison to pledge the funds follows a all-day meeting under the auspices of the IMF.
